introduction-the-ghost-in-the-machine.core: A flaky test passes and fails on the same code. Each flake erodes trust: people learn to hit 're-run', real failures get ignored, and CI time is wasted.

first_principles.problem: Engineers habitually re-run red builds, so a real regression slips through because 'it's probably flaky'.
derivation: **Measure** flakiness (pass/fail on the same commit).
Find **root causes**.
**Quarantine** rather than just retry.
Run **fewer, relevant** tests (TIA).
**Classify** failures probabilistically.

analogy.title: A smoke alarm that goes off randomly
analogy.story: After a few false alarms, people pull out the battery, and then a real fire goes unnoticed.
analogy.breaks: Some flakiness reveals real production race conditions, so don't dismiss it automatically.

example.title: The re-run habit
flow: Real bug red → re-run → flaky pass

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Flakiness is a reliability problem, not a nuisance.

check.a: It produces different results on the same code without any change.

root-causes-of-flakiness-know-your-enemy.core: Most flakes come from a few causes: race conditions and timing (sleeps), shared state and test-order dependence, external dependencies (network, time, randomness) and resource limits on CI runners.

first_principles.problem: You can't fix flakiness without knowing which category it falls into.
derivation: **Timing**: replace sleeps with wait-for-condition.
**Order**: isolate state and randomise order to expose it.
**External**: mock time, seed randomness, stub the network.
**Resources**: right-size runners and avoid hard-coded ports.

analogy.title: Diagnosing an intermittent car fault
analogy.story: It could be wiring (timing), a loose part from a previous repair (shared state), the weather (external) or overload (resources).
analogy.breaks: Some flakes have more than one cause.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: It passes on slow and fast runners alike.

code.text:
# flaky
time.sleep(2); assert page.has_text("Saved")
# robust
page.wait_for_text("Saved", timeout=10)

check.q: Why is sleep() a common source of flakiness?
check.a: Fixed waits are too short on slow machines, and the operation's timing varies from run to run.

handling-flake-retries-vs-quarantine.core: Automatic retries hide flakes and cost time. Quarantine moves known-flaky tests to a non-blocking lane with an owner and a deadline, so CI stays trustworthy while flakes actually get fixed.

first_principles.problem: Blanket retries make CI green but hide growing flakiness and slow every run.
truths: Blocking on flaky tests stalls everyone.
derivation: **Detect**: the test failed then passed on the same commit.
**Quarantine**: run it, but don't block on it.
**Assign an owner** and a ticket with an SLA.
**Un-quarantine** after a period of stability.

analogy.title: Isolating a patient instead of ignoring symptoms
analogy.story: Quarantine protects everyone else while the patient is treated.
analogy.breaks: Quarantine can become a graveyard without SLAs, so track its size.

check.q: Why is quarantine better than blanket retries?
check.a: It keeps the blocking signal trustworthy while making flakes visible and assigned, rather than hidden.

test-impact-analysis-tia-the-smart-scalp.core: Test impact analysis maps tests to the code they exercise (via coverage or the dependency graph), so a change runs only the tests that could be affected. That's faster CI and less exposure to flakes.

first_principles.problem: Running 50,000 tests for a one-line CSS change wastes time and maximises the chance of hitting a flake.
truths: Most tests are unrelated to a given change.
Coverage or dependency data links tests to code.
Fewer tests means fewer flake opportunities.
derivation: Build a **test → code map** (coverage or build graph).
**Diff** the change → affected files.
**Select** the tests touching them.
Run the **full suite periodically** as a safety net.

analogy.title: A surgeon's scalpel instead of a full-body scan
analogy.story: Operate where the problem is, but still do a periodic full check-up.
analogy.breaks: Maps can miss indirect effects (config, reflection), hence the full-suite backstop.

example.title: A one-file change

steps.label: Backstop
steps.detail: The full suite runs nightly on main.

example.outcome: CI scales with the size of the change.

check.q: Why keep running the full suite periodically with TIA?
check.a: Impact maps can miss indirect dependencies, so the full run catches what selection skipped.

probabilistic-failure-analysis-is-it-me-.core: Use history to judge each failure: a test with a known flake rate failing on unrelated code is probably flaky, while a stable test failing right after you touched its code is probably real. Surface that likelihood to developers.

first_principles.problem: Developers either chase flakes as if they were real bugs or dismiss real bugs as flakes.
truths: Each test has a measurable historical failure rate.
Context (files changed) raises or lowers the likelihood.
Better diagnosis saves time both ways.
derivation: Track each test's **historical flake rate**.
Consider **change relevance** (did you touch the code it covers?).
Show a **'likely flaky' or 'likely real'** label.
**Auto-retry only** likely-flaky failures, and flag them.

analogy.title: A doctor weighing symptoms against medical history
analogy.story: A chronic cough in a smoker is different from a sudden cough after a known exposure.
analogy.breaks: Probability isn't certainty. Real regressions can hide in flaky tests.

example.title: Two failures on one PR
flow: test_upload: 8% flake rate, untouched code → likely flaky
test_tax: 0% history, you edited tax.py → likely real

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The developer goes straight to test_tax.

check.q: What two signals help judge whether a failure is real?
check.a: The test's historical flake rate and whether the change touched code the test covers.
